reason: The crank and ratchet look like parts of the winding drum assembly.
expectation: The crank and ratchet will fit onto the drum so it can wind the lifting cord.

effect: The drum and crank form a hand winch; it can now be fitted to the crane.
reaction: The longer crank trading hand travel for turning effect is interesting.
reason: The crane needs the winch to raise its load.
expectation: The hand winch will mount on the crane frame.

effect: The winch is mounted on the crane, ready for the lifting cord.
reaction: That was a straightforward assembly step.
reason: The cord needs to connect the winch to the hook and pulley for lifting.
expectation: The cord and hook will be fitted to the crane's winch and pulley.

effect: The crane now has a lifting line; it still needs a way to hold a raised load.
reason: The pawl and release lever should let the ratchet hold the winch and release it for lowering.
expectation: The pawl and lever will fit to the winch's ratchet.

effect: The pawl can hold the rope, but the crane still needs protection against tipping.
reaction: The distinction between holding the load and stabilizing the crane is useful.
reason: The rear ballast should help counterbalance a load before testing the crane.
expectation: The ballast will fit at the rear to help resist tipping.

effect: The ballast cannot be used yet, so I need to find what the rigged crane can do first.
reaction: I expected the ballast to fit before testing, so that was surprising.
reason: Inspecting the crane should reveal the next available operation.
expectation: The crane will list a compatible item, possibly the test weight.

alternatives.reason: I could try the test weight directly, but checking first may clarify the intended sequence.

effect: The low test showed that the pawl holds the rope, but the crane begins to tip; ballast now looks like the next step.
reaction: The test made the difference between holding and balancing a load clear.
reason: The rear ballast should counter the tipping observed during the test.
expectation: The ballast will stabilize the crane for another lift.

effect: The ballast keeps the feet down in the supported low test, and the pawl holds the drum until released.
reaction: The test clarified how the ballast and pawl do different jobs.
reason: The crane has passed its low test, so the cargo basket is the next likely load.
expectation: The crane will lift the basket, hold it, and lower it gently.

effect: The basket test completed the goal and showed the pawl holding the load while the crank and release lever controlled lowering.
reaction: It was satisfying to see the separate holding and balancing mechanisms work together in a delivery.

mostWorthwhile.text: The supported test and ballast adjustment were most worthwhile: they demonstrated that holding the rope and preventing the crane from tipping are different problems.

leastWorthwhile.text: Trying the ballast before the test was least worthwhile; it could not be fitted yet, despite seeming like a sensible precaution.

surprise.text: I was surprised that the ballast was unavailable until the low test revealed the tipping problem.

arbitrary.text: The required order for fitting the ballast felt somewhat arbitrary: I understood the benefit of testing, but not why it could not be fitted beforehand.

continue.text: Yes. I would try another chapter for the clear mechanical explanations and the opportunity to see another construction tested, though I would hope for fewer hidden sequencing restrictions.
